title: Product plus one
hook: Primes thin out as numbers grow. Could a long enough list hold them all?

knows: that every whole number above 1 breaks into primes (prime recipes)
doesNotKnow: Euclid's argument that the primes never end

misconception: After enough primes you must run out; a long enough list of primes could be complete.
objective: The learner can explain that for any finite list of primes, (product + 1) leaves remainder 1 on division by each listed prime, so its prime factors are missing from the list, and so no list contains every prime.

claims.source: Recomputed with node by trial division; the stage factors with the same trial division.

claims.text: For the lists 2; 2, 3; 2, 3, 5; 2, 3, 5, 7; 2 to 11, product + 1 is 3, 7, 31, 211 and 2311, each prime; product + 1 is not always prime (30031 is not).
claims.source: Trial division up to the square root, recomputed with node.

claims.text: Product + 1 leaves remainder 1 when divided by each prime in the list, so its prime factors are never in the list.
claims.source: The product is a multiple of each listed p, so product + 1 = 1 mod p. Checked with node for all 63 non-empty subsets of 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13: no factor of product + 1 is in its subset.

claims.text: No finite list holds every prime: the primes never run out (Euclid).
claims.source: Euclid, Elements IX.20 (prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers); e.g. Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Theorem 4.

claims.text: Every whole number above 1 has at least one prime factor.
claims.source: Its smallest divisor above 1 is prime (any divisor of it would be a smaller divisor). Used in the reveal's step 'some prime divides it'.

recall.question: Someone claims the list 2, 3, 5, 7 contains every prime. What single number shows them wrong, and how?
options: 211 = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 + 1: none of 2, 3, 5, 7 divides it, so it has a prime factor missing from the list
210 = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7: it is not prime
9: it is odd and not in the list
recall.why: The product + 1 leaves remainder 1 on division by every listed prime, so its prime factors (here 211 itself) are not on the list.
